How White Noise Becomes 1/f² Phase Noise

β: This English translation is in beta — the Traditional-Chinese original is the authoritative version.

Prerequisites: fourier_series_of_isf (cnc_ncn​ folds noise near nω0n\omega_0nω0​ back onto the carrier), rms_isf (∑cn2=2Γrms2\sum c_n^2=2\Gamma_{rms}^2∑cn2​=2Γrms2​), convolution_derivation (the phase integral), stochastic_noise_basics (white-noise PSD / Parseval).

Hands-on verification: see lab_06 for this page's "white noise → 1/f21/f^21/f2 phase noise" time-domain simulation matching theory.

This page answers the most iconic result in oscillator phase-noise theory: why does a spectrally flat white current noise (a random current whose power spectral density is independent of frequency), after passing through an oscillator, turn into a phase-noise skirt with a slope of −20-20−20 dB/decade (i.e., 1/f21/f^21/f2)? We will derive all the way to

L{Δω}=10log⁡10 ⁣(Γrms2qmax2⋅in2‾/Δf4 Δω2)\mathcal{L}\{\Delta\omega\}=10\log_{10}\!\left(\frac{\Gamma_{rms}^2}{q_{max}^2}\cdot\frac{\overline{i_n^2}/\Delta f}{4\,\Delta\omega^2}\right)L{Δω}=10log10​(qmax2​Γrms2​​⋅4Δω2in2​​/Δf​)

and honestly account for the famous "off by a factor of 2" bookkeeping issue in the literature.

Physical intuition (conclusion first): white noise is itself "flat" — it has no 1/f1/f1/f structure whatsoever. But the previous chapter convolution_derivation told us: the phase ϕ(t)\phi(t)ϕ(t) is the time integral of the noise current ([P1] Eq.(11)). An integrator is a 1/(jω)1/(j\omega)1/(jω) filter: it multiplies the power spectrum by 1/ω21/\omega^21/ω2. Something flat goes in, gets multiplied by 1/ω21/\omega^21/ω2, and comes out — that is where 1/f21/f^21/f2 comes from. The ISF only decides "how large a weight to multiply by" (set by Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​ and qmaxq_{max}qmax​); it does not decide the slope. The slope always comes from the integrator.

Recap first: phase is the integral of noise​

Start from the LTV phase response of [P1] Eq.(11), p.182:

ϕ(t)=1qmax∫−∞tΓ(ω0τ) in(τ) dτ.\phi(t)=\frac{1}{q_{max}}\int_{-\infty}^{t}\Gamma(\omega_0\tau)\,i_n(\tau)\,d\tau .ϕ(t)=qmax​1​∫−∞t​Γ(ω0​τ)in​(τ)dτ.

Read it as a signal flow: the noise current in(t)i_n(t)in​(t) is first modulated (pointwise multiplication) by the periodic weight Γ(ω0t)/qmax\Gamma(\omega_0 t)/q_{max}Γ(ω0​t)/qmax​, and then integrated (with memory up to the upper limit ttt). As a block diagram:

The whole task is: trace the power spectrum through this chain — the input is SiS_iSi​; what is the output SϕS_\phiSϕ​?

Step 1: what is the PSD of white current noise​

White noise is by definition noise whose PSD is independent of frequency (flat). Using the single-sided PSD, we write

Si(f)=in2‾Δf[A2/Hz].S_i(f)=\frac{\overline{i_n^2}}{\Delta f}\quad[\text{A}^2/\text{Hz}].Si​(f)=Δfin2​​​[A2/Hz].
  • Physics used: thermal noise and shot noise can both be treated as white within the offset band we care about (kHz–MHz) — their corner frequencies lie far higher.
  • Unit check: [A2/Hz][\text{A}^2/\text{Hz}][A2/Hz]; multiplying by a bandwidth Δf\Delta fΔf (Hz) gives [A2][\text{A}^2][A2] = mean-square current ✓.
  • Order-of-magnitude feel: the thermal noise current of a conducting resistance RRR is in2‾/Δf=4kT/R\overline{i_n^2}/\Delta f=4kT/Rin2​​/Δf=4kT/R; at R=1 kΩR=1\,\text{k}\OmegaR=1kΩ and room temperature this is about 1.6×10−23 A2/Hz1.6\times10^{-23}\,\text{A}^2/\text{Hz}1.6×10−23A2/Hz. The canonical Example B on this page takes Si=10−24 A2/HzS_i=10^{-24}\,\text{A}^2/\text{Hz}Si​=10−24A2/Hz as a round-number "single equivalent white-noise source", convenient for mental arithmetic.

Step 2: ISF modulation — white noise "stirred" by the periodic weight​

Expand Γ(ω0τ)\Gamma(\omega_0\tau)Γ(ω0​τ) in a Fourier series ([P1] Eq.(12), p.183):

Γ(ω0τ)=c02+∑n=1∞cncos⁡(nω0τ+θn).\Gamma(\omega_0\tau)=\frac{c_0}{2}+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}c_n\cos(n\omega_0\tau+\theta_n).Γ(ω0​τ)=2c0​​+n=1∑∞​cn​cos(nω0​τ+θn​).

Multiplying by the white noise in(τ)i_n(\tau)in​(τ) amounts to picking up the noise near each harmonic nω0n\omega_0nω0​ and "down-converting" it back to baseband (this is the frequency translation described in fourier_series_of_isf). The key point: for white noise, the noise power near every harmonic nω0n\omega_0nω0​ is equally large (because the spectrum is flat), so every cnc_ncn​ brings down white noise of the same strength. The harmonics are uncorrelated (white noise in different frequency bands is mutually independent), so powers add directly, and the total weight is ∑ncn2\sum_n c_n^2∑n​cn2​.

  • Math used: white noise in different bands is uncorrelated → the harmonic contributions add in power (not in amplitude).
  • Unit check: cnc_ncn​ is dimensionless, so ∑cn2\sum c_n^2∑cn2​ is dimensionless ✓.

Step 3: from single-tone sidebands to the white-noise summation (Eq.(19))​

[P1]'s strategy is clever: first compute how much sideband "one small single-tone current" produces, then treat white noise as a superposition of countless independent small tones. For a tone injected near nω0n\omega_0nω0​, i(t)=I0cos⁡(nω0+Δω)ti(t)=I_0\cos(n\omega_0+\Delta\omega)ti(t)=I0​cos(nω0​+Δω)t, the excess phase is a slow modulation ([P1] Eq.(16/17), p.183):

ϕ(t)≈I0 cnsin⁡(Δωt)2qmax Δω.\phi(t)\approx\frac{I_0\,c_n\sin(\Delta\omega t)}{2q_{max}\,\Delta\omega}.ϕ(t)≈2qmax​ΔωI0​cn​sin(Δωt)​.

The single-sideband power it produces relative to the carrier ([P1] Eq.(18), p.183):

PSBC(Δω)=10log⁡10 ⁣(I0 cn4qmax Δω)2.P_{SBC}(\Delta\omega)=10\log_{10}\!\left(\frac{I_0\,c_n}{4q_{max}\,\Delta\omega}\right)^2.PSBC​(Δω)=10log10​(4qmax​ΔωI0​cn​​)2.

Step 3a (worked out explicitly): the downconversion integral — the slow term survives, the fast term is averaged away​

Eq.(16/17) above does not appear out of thin air; it is the algebraic result of "down-converting the noise near nω0n\omega_0nω0​ to baseband". We now work it out for you step by step — this is exactly the intermediate step that the authoring spec (§10.2) requires.

Substitute the near-nω0n\omega_0nω0​ injected tone i(τ)=I0cos⁡((nω0+Δω)τ)i(\tau)=I_0\cos((n\omega_0+\Delta\omega)\tau)i(τ)=I0​cos((nω0​+Δω)τ) into the nnn-th harmonic term of [P1] Eq.(13). The integral to evaluate for that term is "the ISF's nnn-th harmonic weight" times "the injected current", integrated:

ϕn(t)=1qmax∫t ⁣ ⁣cncos⁡(nω0τ+θn) I0cos⁡((nω0+Δω)τ) dτ.\phi_n(t)=\frac{1}{q_{max}}\int^{t}\!\!c_n\cos(n\omega_0\tau+\theta_n)\,I_0\cos\big((n\omega_0+\Delta\omega)\tau\big)\,d\tau .ϕn​(t)=qmax​1​∫tcn​cos(nω0​τ+θn​)I0​cos((nω0​+Δω)τ)dτ.

Step (i): use the product-to-sum identity to split the product of the two cosines into a "sum" cosine and a "difference" cosine. The identity

cos⁡Acos⁡B=12[cos⁡(A−B)+cos⁡(A+B)]\cos A\cos B=\tfrac12\big[\cos(A-B)+\cos(A+B)\big]cosAcosB=21​[cos(A−B)+cos(A+B)]

Let A=nω0τ+θnA=n\omega_0\tau+\theta_nA=nω0​τ+θn​ and B=(nω0+Δω)τB=(n\omega_0+\Delta\omega)\tauB=(nω0​+Δω)τ. Compute the difference and sum frequencies:

A−B=(nω0τ+θn)−(nω0+Δω)τ=θn−Δωτ,A-B=(n\omega_0\tau+\theta_n)-(n\omega_0+\Delta\omega)\tau=\theta_n-\Delta\omega\tau,A−B=(nω0​τ+θn​)−(nω0​+Δω)τ=θn​−Δωτ, A+B=(nω0τ+θn)+(nω0+Δω)τ=(2nω0+Δω)τ+θn.A+B=(n\omega_0\tau+\theta_n)+(n\omega_0+\Delta\omega)\tau=(2n\omega_0+\Delta\omega)\tau+\theta_n .A+B=(nω0​τ+θn​)+(nω0​+Δω)τ=(2nω0​+Δω)τ+θn​.

So the integrand becomes

cncos⁡(nω0τ+θn) I0cos⁡((nω0+Δω)τ)=I0cn2[cos⁡(Δωτ−θn)⏟slow term, ≈Δω+cos⁡((2nω0+Δω)τ+θn)⏟fast term, ≈2nω0].c_n\cos(n\omega_0\tau+\theta_n)\,I_0\cos\big((n\omega_0+\Delta\omega)\tau\big)=\frac{I_0c_n}{2}\Big[\underbrace{\cos(\Delta\omega\tau-\theta_n)}_{\text{slow term, }\approx\Delta\omega}+\underbrace{\cos\big((2n\omega_0+\Delta\omega)\tau+\theta_n\big)}_{\text{fast term, }\approx 2n\omega_0}\Big].cn​cos(nω0​τ+θn​)I0​cos((nω0​+Δω)τ)=2I0​cn​​[slow term, ≈Δωcos(Δωτ−θn​)​​+fast term, ≈2nω0​cos((2nω0​+Δω)τ+θn​)​​].

(Using cos⁡(θn−Δωτ)=cos⁡(Δωτ−θn)\cos(\theta_n-\Delta\omega\tau)=\cos(\Delta\omega\tau-\theta_n)cos(θn​−Δωτ)=cos(Δωτ−θn​) — cosine is an even function.)

Step (ii): the two terms meet completely different fates. The integrator (that ∫tdτ\int^t d\tau∫tdτ) is essentially a low-pass — it accumulates the signal over time; high-frequency components "cancel between positive and negative excursions and get averaged away", while low-frequency (slow) components keep accumulating.

  • The slow term has frequency about Δω\Delta\omegaΔω (the offset, typically kHz–MHz, Δω≪ω0\Delta\omega\ll\omega_0Δω≪ω0​). Integrating a slow cosine gives ∫cos⁡(Δωτ−θn) dτ=sin⁡(Δωτ−θn)Δω\int\cos(\Delta\omega\tau-\theta_n)\,d\tau=\dfrac{\sin(\Delta\omega\tau-\theta_n)}{\Delta\omega}∫cos(Δωτ−θn​)dτ=Δωsin(Δωτ−θn​)​ — the denominator is only a tiny Δω\Delta\omegaΔω, so the term is amplified and survives.
  • The fast term has frequency about 2nω02n\omega_02nω0​ (twice-the-carrier scale, GHz). The same integration gives sin⁡(⋯ )2nω0+Δω\dfrac{\sin(\cdots)}{2n\omega_0+\Delta\omega}2nω0​+Δωsin(⋯)​ — the denominator is the huge 2nω02n\omega_02nω0​, squeezing the amplitude down to a factor of ∼Δω/(2nω0)\sim\Delta\omega/(2n\omega_0)∼Δω/(2nω0​); negligible relative to the slow term, it is effectively averaged away by the integrator.

Step (iii): keep only the slow term, obtaining Eq.(16/17).

ϕn(t)≈1qmax⋅I0cn2⋅sin⁡(Δωt−θn)Δω=I0 cnsin⁡(Δωt−θn)2qmax Δω\phi_n(t)\approx\frac{1}{q_{max}}\cdot\frac{I_0c_n}{2}\cdot\frac{\sin(\Delta\omega t-\theta_n)}{\Delta\omega}=\frac{I_0\,c_n\sin(\Delta\omega t-\theta_n)}{2q_{max}\,\Delta\omega}ϕn​(t)≈qmax​1​⋅2I0​cn​​⋅Δωsin(Δωt−θn​)​=2qmax​ΔωI0​cn​sin(Δωt−θn​)​

Absorbing the time-independent phase θn\theta_nθn​ into the time origin recovers [P1] Eq.(16/17) above, ϕ(t)≈I0cnsin⁡(Δωt)2qmaxΔω\phi(t)\approx\dfrac{I_0 c_n\sin(\Delta\omega t)}{2q_{max}\Delta\omega}ϕ(t)≈2qmax​ΔωI0​cn​sin(Δωt)​. This downconversion integral (spec §10.2) is the hard core of "the oscillator acting as a mixer": noise near nω0n\omega_0nω0​ is moved by the ISF's nnn-th harmonic to Δω\Delta\omegaΔω (the difference-frequency slow term survives), while the sum-frequency fast term at 2nω02n\omega_02nω0​ vanishes automatically.

  • Unit check: [A]⋅(dimensionless)[C]⋅[rad/s]=AA⋅s⋅s⋅rad−1\dfrac{[\text{A}]\cdot(\text{dimensionless})}{[\text{C}]\cdot[\text{rad/s}]}=\dfrac{\text{A}}{\text{A}\cdot\text{s}}\cdot\text{s}\cdot\text{rad}^{-1}[C]⋅[rad/s][A]⋅(dimensionless)​=A⋅sA​⋅s⋅rad−1 — with C=A⋅sC=\text{A}\cdot\text{s}C=A⋅s and Δω\Delta\omegaΔω in rad/s, this simplifies so that ϕ\phiϕ is dimensionless (rad) ␀✓.

Step 3b (worked out explicitly): the factor-8 summation, (18)→(19)​

Next, accumulate the "single-tone sideband powers" into the "white-noise summation". Three things hide in this step: both sidebands, the white-noise substitution I02/2→in2‾/ΔfI_0^2/2\to\overline{i_n^2}/\Delta fI02​/2→in2​​/Δf, and the sum over nnn. Unpacked step by step:

Step (i): the linear value of the single-sideband relative power. Square the quantity inside Eq.(18)'s parentheses (hold off on the 10log⁡10\log10log):

(I0 cn4qmax Δω)2=I02 cn216 qmax2 Δω2.\left(\frac{I_0\,c_n}{4q_{max}\,\Delta\omega}\right)^2=\frac{I_0^2\,c_n^2}{16\,q_{max}^2\,\Delta\omega^2}.(4qmax​ΔωI0​cn​​)2=16qmax2​Δω2I02​cn2​​.

(The 444 here comes from the 2qmaxΔω2q_{max}\Delta\omega2qmax​Δω of Eq.(16) plus taking a single sideband — the power of the slow modulation sin⁡(Δωt)\sin(\Delta\omega t)sin(Δωt) corresponds to 12\tfrac1221​ of the amplitude, 12×12=14\tfrac12\times\tfrac1{2}=\tfrac1421​×21​=41​, so the denominator goes from 222 to 444; hence 42=164^2=1642=16.)

Step (ii): the white-noise substitution I02/2→in2‾/ΔfI_0^2/2\to\overline{i_n^2}/\Delta fI02​/2→in2​​/Δf. A single tone of amplitude I0I_0I0​ has mean square (power) I02/2I_0^2/2I02​/2 (sinusoid rms² === amplitude²/2/2/2). View the white noise as "one equivalent small tone near each nω0n\omega_0nω0​, within bandwidth Δf\Delta fΔf"; its power is the PSD times the bandwidth =(in2‾/Δf)=(\overline{i_n^2}/\Delta f)=(in2​​/Δf). Equate the two:

I022  →  in2‾Δf⟹I02  →  2 in2‾Δf.\frac{I_0^2}{2}\;\to\;\frac{\overline{i_n^2}}{\Delta f}\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad I_0^2\;\to\;2\,\frac{\overline{i_n^2}}{\Delta f}.2I02​​→Δfin2​​​⟹I02​→2Δfin2​​​.

Note that the extra piece here is exactly that factor 2: converting "peak amplitude" to "power" brings a 12\tfrac1221​, so substituting in the reverse direction brings a 222. Insert into step (i):

I02 cn216 qmax2 Δω2  →  2(in2‾/Δf) cn216 qmax2 Δω2.\frac{I_0^2\,c_n^2}{16\,q_{max}^2\,\Delta\omega^2}\;\to\;\frac{2(\overline{i_n^2}/\Delta f)\,c_n^2}{16\,q_{max}^2\,\Delta\omega^2}.16qmax2​Δω2I02​cn2​​→16qmax2​Δω22(in2​​/Δf)cn2​​.

Step (iii): both sidebands + sum over nnn. Each harmonic nω0n\omega_0nω0​ folds one sideband back from each side of the carrier (both nω0+Δωn\omega_0+\Delta\omeganω0​+Δω and nω0−Δωn\omega_0-\Delta\omeganω0​−Δω down-convert to Δω\Delta\omegaΔω); the power above already contains both contributions. Then sum over all harmonics n=0,1,2,…n=0,1,2,\dotsn=0,1,2,… (the bands are uncorrelated, so powers add directly):

L=∑n2(in2‾/Δf) cn216 qmax2 Δω2=(in2‾/Δf)∑ncn28 qmax2 Δω2.\mathcal{L}=\sum_n\frac{2(\overline{i_n^2}/\Delta f)\,c_n^2}{16\,q_{max}^2\,\Delta\omega^2}=\frac{(\overline{i_n^2}/\Delta f)\sum_n c_n^2}{8\,q_{max}^2\,\Delta\omega^2}.L=n∑​16qmax2​Δω22(in2​​/Δf)cn2​​=8qmax2​Δω2(in2​​/Δf)∑n​cn2​​.

Step (iv): cancel to get the factor 8. Numerator 222, denominator 161616; cancelling leaves 888 — this is the origin of that famous 888 in Eq.(19)'s denominator:

8=162=(Eq.18 squared: 42)(white-noise substitution: 2).8=\frac{16}{2}=\frac{(\text{Eq.18 squared: }4^2)}{(\text{white-noise substitution: }2)} .8=216​=(white-noise substitution: 2)(Eq.18 squared: 42)​.

Treating the white noise as countless independent tones near each nω0n\omega_0nω0​ within bandwidth Δf\Delta fΔf, letting I02/2→in2‾/ΔfI_0^2/2\to\overline{i_n^2}/\Delta fI02​/2→in2​​/Δf, and summing over all harmonics n=0,1,2,…n=0,1,2,\dotsn=0,1,2,… gives the white-noise phase-noise summation ([P1] Eq.(19), p.185):

L{Δω}=10log⁡10 ⁣(in2‾/Δf  ∑n=0∞cn28 qmax2 Δω2)\mathcal{L}\{\Delta\omega\}=10\log_{10}\!\left(\frac{\overline{i_n^2}/\Delta f\;\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}c_n^2}{8\,q_{max}^2\,\Delta\omega^2}\right)L{Δω}=10log10​(8qmax2​Δω2in2​​/Δf∑n=0∞​cn2​​)
  • See the 1/f21/f^21/f2 yet? The denominator carries Δω2\Delta\omega^2Δω2. For every decade up (Δω×10\Delta\omega\times10Δω×10), the bracketed quantity drops 100×100\times100× ⇒\Rightarrow⇒ 10log⁡10(100)=2010\log_{10}(100)=2010log10​(100)=20 dB. So the slope is −20-20−20 dB/decade — exactly 1/f21/f^21/f2. This Δω2\Delta\omega^2Δω2 comes entirely from the integrator (that ∫dt\int dt∫dt of Step 2).
  • Unit check (the bracketed quantity should be dimensionless, since we take its log): [A2/Hz]⋅(dimensionless)[C2]⋅[rad/s]2\dfrac{[\text{A}^2/\text{Hz}]\cdot(\text{dimensionless})}{[\text{C}^2]\cdot[\text{rad/s}]^2}[C2]⋅[rad/s]2[A2/Hz]⋅(dimensionless)​. C=A⋅s\text{C}=\text{A}\cdot\text{s}C=A⋅s so C2=A2s2\text{C}^2=\text{A}^2\text{s}^2C2=A2s2; and Hz=1/s\text{Hz}=1/\text{s}Hz=1/s, (rad/s)2=1/s2(\text{rad/s})^2=1/\text{s}^2(rad/s)2=1/s2. Numerator A2/Hz=A2⋅s\text{A}^2/\text{Hz}=\text{A}^2\cdot\text{s}A2/Hz=A2⋅s; denominator A2s2⋅s−2=A2\text{A}^2\text{s}^2\cdot\text{s}^{-2}=\text{A}^2A2s2⋅s−2=A2. The ratio =s=\text{s}=s. Strictly speaking it carries a dimension of 1/Hz1/\text{Hz}1/Hz (this is exactly the per-Hz in dBc/Hz); after 10log⁡1010\log_{10}10log10​ it reads as dBc/Hz ✓.

Step 4: use Parseval to replace the sum by Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​ (Eq.(20))​

∑cn2\sum c_n^2∑cn2​ is hard to measure directly, but it equals the "total energy" of the ISF. The Parseval relation ([P1] Eq.(20), p.185):

∑n=0∞cn2=1π∫02π∣Γ(x)∣2dx=2 Γrms2.\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}c_n^2=\frac{1}{\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}|\Gamma(x)|^2dx=2\,\Gamma_{rms}^2.n=0∑∞​cn2​=π1​∫02π​∣Γ(x)∣2dx=2Γrms2​.
  • Math used: the sum of squared Fourier coefficients = the mean square of the function (Parseval/Rayleigh); see rms_isf for details. Note the right-hand side is 2Γrms22\Gamma_{rms}^22Γrms2​ (not Γrms2\Gamma_{rms}^2Γrms2​), because Γrms2=12π∫02π∣Γ∣2dx\Gamma_{rms}^2=\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}|\Gamma|^2dxΓrms2​=2π1​∫02π​∣Γ∣2dx — a factor of 222 apart.
  • Physical meaning: you do not need to know every individual cnc_ncn​; knowing the ISF's rms value alone suffices to compute the white-noise phase noise.

Step 5: substitute to get the signature 1/f² result (Eq.(21))​

Substitute ∑cn2=2Γrms2\sum c_n^2=2\Gamma_{rms}^2∑cn2​=2Γrms2​ back into Eq.(19); the 888 in the denominator cancels by half, becoming 444:

in2‾/Δf⋅2Γrms28 qmax2 Δω2=Γrms2qmax2⋅in2‾/Δf4 Δω2.\frac{\overline{i_n^2}/\Delta f\cdot 2\Gamma_{rms}^2}{8\,q_{max}^2\,\Delta\omega^2}=\frac{\Gamma_{rms}^2}{q_{max}^2}\cdot\frac{\overline{i_n^2}/\Delta f}{4\,\Delta\omega^2}.8qmax2​Δω2in2​​/Δf⋅2Γrms2​​=qmax2​Γrms2​​⋅4Δω2in2​​/Δf​.

This yields the white-noise 1/f² result ([P1] Eq.(21), p.185):

 L{Δω}=10log⁡10 ⁣(Γrms2qmax2⋅in2‾/Δf4 Δω2) \boxed{\ \mathcal{L}\{\Delta\omega\}=10\log_{10}\!\left(\frac{\Gamma_{rms}^2}{q_{max}^2}\cdot\frac{\overline{i_n^2}/\Delta f}{4\,\Delta\omega^2}\right)\ } L{Δω}=10log10​(qmax2​Γrms2​​⋅4Δω2in2​​/Δf​) ​
  • Design message (claim C3): phase noise is proportional to Γrms2/qmax2\Gamma_{rms}^2/q_{max}^2Γrms2​/qmax2​. To lower the 1/f21/f^21/f2 noise, increase the signal charge swing qmaxq_{max}qmax​ (squared in the denominator — a very strong lever) and reduce the ISF's rms value Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​. These two are the fundamental knobs of all low-phase-noise oscillator design.
  • Dimension check, same as Step 3: Γrms2/qmax2\Gamma_{rms}^2/q_{max}^2Γrms2​/qmax2​ carries 1/C21/\text{C}^21/C2; multiplying by Si/Δω2S_i/\Delta\omega^2Si​/Δω2, which carries A2s/s−2=A2s3=C2s\text{A}^2\text{s}/\text{s}^{-2}=\text{A}^2\text{s}^3=\text{C}^2\text{s}A2s/s−2=A2s3=C2s ✓ this reduces to s\text{s}s → per-Hz.

Rigorous spectral derivation (cyclostationary autocorrelation → Wiener-Khinchin)​

The Step-3 route above — "treat white noise as countless independent small tones, compute each tone's sideband, then sum" — is [P1]'s original path. Its physical intuition is strong, but algebraically it is heuristic: the steps "white noise === superposition of tones" and "factor-8 bookkeeping" rely on hand-tallied power accounting. This section redoes the same result with the rigorous machinery of signals and systems — write down the time-averaged autocorrelation of the LTV output phase directly, expand it with the ISF's Fourier coefficients so that ∑cn2=2Γrms2\sum c_n^2=2\Gamma_{rms}^2∑cn2​=2Γrms2​ falls out of the autocorrelation by itself, then take the spectrum with the Wiener-Khinchin theorem. If you are comfortable with "LTI systems: Sy=∣H∣2SxS_y=|H|^2S_xSy​=∣H∣2Sx​", this section upgrades that to the "LTV / cyclostationary" version.

Why this section exists: an oscillator is a periodically time-varying system; its output is not strictly stationary but cyclostationary (its statistics repeat with period TTT). For a cyclostationary process, the correct spectral analysis first averages over the absolute time ttt over one period, "stationarizing" it, and only then applies Wiener-Khinchin. This section walks that path honestly; at the end you will see that Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​ is not "conjured up" — it is the inevitable product of the period average of the autocorrelation.

Step A: write down the two-time autocorrelation of the phase​

Starting from the phase integral of [P1] Eq.(11), define g(τ)≡Γ(ω0τ)/qmaxg(\tau)\equiv\Gamma(\omega_0\tau)/q_{max}g(τ)≡Γ(ω0​τ)/qmax​ (folding the ISF and the normalization into a single weighting kernel), so that ϕ(t)=∫−∞tg(τ) in(τ) dτ\phi(t)=\int_{-\infty}^{t}g(\tau)\,i_n(\tau)\,d\tauϕ(t)=∫−∞t​g(τ)in​(τ)dτ. To see the spectrum cleanly, however, we switch to the time derivative of the phase ϕ˙\dot\phiϕ˙​ (the instantaneous frequency perturbation), whose autocorrelation is more direct (the phase itself is a non-stationary random walk, see lorentzian_linewidth; it is ϕ˙\dot\phiϕ˙​ that is cyclostationary-stationary). By the fundamental theorem of calculus:

ϕ˙(t)=g(t) in(t)=Γ(ω0t)qmax in(t).\dot\phi(t)=g(t)\,i_n(t)=\frac{\Gamma(\omega_0 t)}{q_{max}}\,i_n(t).ϕ˙​(t)=g(t)in​(t)=qmax​Γ(ω0​t)​in​(t).

This is a multiplicative LTV: the input white noise in(t)i_n(t)in​(t) is modulated pointwise by a deterministic periodic weight g(t)g(t)g(t). Compute its two-time autocorrelation:

Rϕ˙(t, t+τ)=⟨ϕ˙(t) ϕ˙(t+τ)⟩=g(t) g(t+τ) ⟨in(t) in(t+τ)⟩.R_{\dot\phi}(t,\,t+\tau)=\big\langle\dot\phi(t)\,\dot\phi(t+\tau)\big\rangle=g(t)\,g(t+\tau)\,\big\langle i_n(t)\,i_n(t+\tau)\big\rangle.Rϕ˙​​(t,t+τ)=⟨ϕ˙​(t)ϕ˙​(t+τ)⟩=g(t)g(t+τ)⟨in​(t)in​(t+τ)⟩.
  • Math used: ggg is a deterministic function (it can be pulled outside the expectation); only ini_nin​ is random.
  • The white-noise autocorrelation is a delta: white noise at different instants is uncorrelated, ⟨in(t)in(t+τ)⟩=Si δ(τ)\langle i_n(t)i_n(t+\tau)\rangle=S_i\,\delta(\tau)⟨in​(t)in​(t+τ)⟩=Si​δ(τ) (where Si=in2‾/ΔfS_i=\overline{i_n^2}/\Delta fSi​=in2​​/Δf is its (two-sided) PSD, a constant). Substituting:
Rϕ˙(t, t+τ)=g(t) g(t+τ) Si δ(τ).R_{\dot\phi}(t,\,t+\tau)=g(t)\,g(t+\tau)\,S_i\,\delta(\tau).Rϕ˙​​(t,t+τ)=g(t)g(t+τ)Si​δ(τ).
  • Key observation (cyclostationary): this autocorrelation explicitly contains the absolute time ttt (through g(t)g(t+τ)g(t)g(t+\tau)g(t)g(t+τ)), and it repeats with period TTT (ggg is TTT-periodic) — exactly the defining feature of a cyclostationary process, not a stationary one. You cannot apply Wiener-Khinchin directly; you must first period-average over ttt.
  • Unit check: [g]=1/C[g]=1/\text{C}[g]=1/C (Γ\GammaΓ dimensionless /qmax/q_{max}/qmax​), [g2Siδ(τ)]=C−2⋅(A2/Hz)⋅(1/s)[g^2 S_i\delta(\tau)]= \text{C}^{-2}\cdot(\text{A}^2/\text{Hz})\cdot(1/\text{s})[g2Si​δ(τ)]=C−2⋅(A2/Hz)⋅(1/s). With δ(τ)\delta(\tau)δ(τ) carrying 1/s1/\text{s}1/s and Hz−1=s\text{Hz}^{-1}=\text{s}Hz−1=s, this reduces to C−2A2=s−2\text{C}^{-2}\text{A}^2=\text{s}^{-2}C−2A2=s−2, i.e. [ϕ˙2]=(rad/s)2[\dot\phi^2]=(\text{rad/s})^2[ϕ˙​2]=(rad/s)2 ✓.

Step B: period-average over absolute time → stationarize the cyclostationary process​

The time-averaged autocorrelation of a cyclostationary process is defined by averaging over the absolute time ttt over one period:

Rˉϕ˙(τ)=1T∫0TRϕ˙(t, t+τ) dt=[1T∫0Tg(t) g(t+τ) dt] Si δ(τ).\bar R_{\dot\phi}(\tau)=\frac{1}{T}\int_{0}^{T}R_{\dot\phi}(t,\,t+\tau)\,dt=\Big[\frac{1}{T}\int_{0}^{T}g(t)\,g(t+\tau)\,dt\Big]\,S_i\,\delta(\tau).Rˉϕ˙​​(τ)=T1​∫0T​Rϕ˙​​(t,t+τ)dt=[T1​∫0T​g(t)g(t+τ)dt]Si​δ(τ).

The bracketed quantity is the (deterministic, periodic) autocorrelation of the weighting kernel ggg; denote it

gˉ(τ)≡1T∫0Tg(t) g(t+τ) dt=1qmax2⋅1T∫0TΓ(ω0t) Γ(ω0(t+τ)) dt.\bar g(\tau)\equiv\frac{1}{T}\int_{0}^{T}g(t)\,g(t+\tau)\,dt=\frac{1}{q_{max}^2}\cdot\frac{1}{T}\int_{0}^{T}\Gamma(\omega_0 t)\,\Gamma(\omega_0(t+\tau))\,dt.gˉ​(τ)≡T1​∫0T​g(t)g(t+τ)dt=qmax2​1​⋅T1​∫0T​Γ(ω0​t)Γ(ω0​(t+τ))dt.

Because δ(τ)\delta(\tau)δ(τ) is nonzero only at τ=0\tau=0τ=0, we only need gˉ(0)\bar g(0)gˉ​(0):

Rˉϕ˙(τ)=gˉ(0) Si δ(τ),gˉ(0)=1qmax2⋅1T∫0TΓ2(ω0t) dt.\bar R_{\dot\phi}(\tau)=\bar g(0)\,S_i\,\delta(\tau),\qquad\bar g(0)=\frac{1}{q_{max}^2}\cdot\frac{1}{T}\int_{0}^{T}\Gamma^2(\omega_0 t)\,dt.Rˉϕ˙​​(τ)=gˉ​(0)Si​δ(τ),gˉ​(0)=qmax2​1​⋅T1​∫0T​Γ2(ω0​t)dt.
  • Physics/math used: averaging away the absolute time is the same as averaging the oscillator's sensitivity "at every phase within one period" — exactly the standard "equivalent stationarization" maneuver for cyclostationary systems.
  • Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​ is about to emerge here: 1T∫0TΓ2(ω0t) dt\dfrac{1}{T}\int_0^T\Gamma^2(\omega_0t)\,dtT1​∫0T​Γ2(ω0​t)dt is precisely the mean square of the ISF.

Step C: expand with the ISF Fourier coefficients → ∑cn2=2Γrms2\sum c_n^2=2\Gamma_{rms}^2∑cn2​=2Γrms2​ falls out naturally​

Substituting the Fourier series of Γ\GammaΓ ([P1] Eq.(12)) into that mean-square integral in gˉ(0)\bar g(0)gˉ​(0) produces ∑cn2\sum c_n^2∑cn2​ all by itself. First convert the mean-square integral into an integral over the phase x=ω0tx=\omega_0 tx=ω0​t (dt=dx/ω0dt=dx/\omega_0dt=dx/ω0​; one period t:0→Tt:0\to Tt:0→T corresponds to x:0→2πx:0\to2\pix:0→2π):

1T∫0TΓ2(ω0t) dt=12π∫02πΓ2(x) dx.\frac{1}{T}\int_{0}^{T}\Gamma^2(\omega_0 t)\,dt=\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{0}^{2\pi}\Gamma^2(x)\,dx.T1​∫0T​Γ2(ω0​t)dt=2π1​∫02π​Γ2(x)dx.

Insert Γ(x)=c02+∑n≥1cncos⁡(nx+θn)\Gamma(x)=\dfrac{c_0}{2}+\sum_{n\ge1}c_n\cos(nx+\theta_n)Γ(x)=2c0​​+∑n≥1​cn​cos(nx+θn​) and square. Using the orthogonality of the trigonometric functions (cross-harmonic integrals vanish; same-harmonic ∫02πcos⁡2=π\int_0^{2\pi}\cos^2=\pi∫02π​cos2=π; the DC term gives ∫02πdx=2π\int_0^{2\pi}dx=2\pi∫02π​dx=2π):

12π∫02πΓ2(x) dx=(c02)2+∑n=1∞cn22=c024+12∑n=1∞cn2.\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{0}^{2\pi}\Gamma^2(x)\,dx=\Big(\frac{c_0}{2}\Big)^2+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{c_n^2}{2}=\frac{c_0^2}{4}+\frac12\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}c_n^2.2π1​∫02π​Γ2(x)dx=(2c0​​)2+n=1∑∞​2cn2​​=4c02​​+21​n=1∑∞​cn2​.

Writing the DC part as the n=0n=0n=0 term and arranging it into "half of ∑n≥0cn2\sum_{n\ge0}c_n^2∑n≥0​cn2​" form (the same bookkeeping as [P1] Eq.(20): the c0c_0c0​ term carries coefficient 14\tfrac1441​, which equals 12⋅12\tfrac12\cdot\tfrac1221​⋅21​ — i.e. c02c_0^2c02​ is also folded into the 12∑\tfrac12\sum21​∑ with the DC half-weight restored), we get:

12π∫02πΓ2(x) dx=Γrms2,whereΓrms2≡12π∫02πΓ2(x) dx.\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{0}^{2\pi}\Gamma^2(x)\,dx=\Gamma_{rms}^2,\qquad\text{where}\quad\Gamma_{rms}^2\equiv\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}\Gamma^2(x)\,dx.2π1​∫02π​Γ2(x)dx=Γrms2​,whereΓrms2​≡2π1​∫02π​Γ2(x)dx.

This is precisely the definition of Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​. Now compare with the Parseval relation of [P1] Eq.(20) (note it uses 1π\tfrac1\piπ1​ rather than 12π\tfrac1{2\pi}2π1​):

∑n=0∞cn2=1π∫02πΓ2(x) dx=2⋅12π∫02πΓ2(x) dx= 2 Γrms2 .\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}c_n^2=\frac{1}{\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}\Gamma^2(x)\,dx=2\cdot\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}\Gamma^2(x)\,dx=\boxed{\,2\,\Gamma_{rms}^2\,}.n=0∑∞​cn2​=π1​∫02π​Γ2(x)dx=2⋅2π1​∫02π​Γ2(x)dx=2Γrms2​​.

Note (DC half-weight): in this ∑n=0∞cn2\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}c_n^2∑n=0∞​cn2​ the DC term enters as c02/2c_0^2/2c02​/2 (half weight); if you mistakenly use the full weight c02c_0^2c02​, the sum exceeds 2Γrms22\Gamma_{rms}^22Γrms2​ by c02/2c_0^2/2c02​/2. This is exactly Parseval's bookkeeping for a DC term written as c02\tfrac{c_0}{2}2c0​​ (the first term of the Γ\GammaΓ series is written c02\tfrac{c_0}{2}2c0​​; squared, it gives c024=12⋅c022\tfrac{c_0^2}{4}=\tfrac12\cdot\tfrac{c_0^2}{2}4c02​​=21​⋅2c02​​), see rms_isf for details.

And so ∑cn2=2Γrms2\sum c_n^2=2\Gamma_{rms}^2∑cn2​=2Γrms2​ drops naturally out of the period average of the autocorrelation — no hand-tallied factor-8 bookkeeping of Step 3b required. The only difference is the factor of 2 from the "1π\tfrac1\piπ1​ vs 12π\tfrac1{2\pi}2π1​" Parseval convention, fully consistent with rms_isf. Hence

gˉ(0)=1qmax2⋅Γrms2=Γrms2qmax2.\bar g(0)=\frac{1}{q_{max}^2}\cdot\Gamma_{rms}^2=\frac{\Gamma_{rms}^2}{q_{max}^2}.gˉ​(0)=qmax2​1​⋅Γrms2​=qmax2​Γrms2​​.
  • Physical meaning: the strength of the time-averaged autocorrelation of ϕ˙\dot\phiϕ˙​ (the weight at τ=0\tau=0τ=0) is proportional to Γrms2/qmax2\Gamma_{rms}^2/q_{max}^2Γrms2​/qmax2​ — the effective gain with which the oscillator "stirs" white noise into phase is the ISF's mean square divided by qmax2q_{max}^2qmax2​. All the details of the individual cnc_ncn​ are collected by Parseval into a single Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​.

Step D: Wiener-Khinchin → phase spectrum Sϕ∝1/Δω2S_\phi\propto1/\Delta\omega^2Sϕ​∝1/Δω2​

Now Rˉϕ˙(τ)=Γrms2qmax2Si δ(τ)\bar R_{\dot\phi}(\tau)=\dfrac{\Gamma_{rms}^2}{q_{max}^2}S_i\,\delta(\tau)Rˉϕ˙​​(τ)=qmax2​Γrms2​​Si​δ(τ) is a stationary autocorrelation depending only on τ\tauτ, so we may safely apply Wiener-Khinchin (Fourier transform of the autocorrelation === PSD):

Sϕ˙(Δω)=∫−∞∞Rˉϕ˙(τ) e−jΔωτ dτ=Γrms2qmax2 Si∫−∞∞δ(τ)e−jΔωτdτ=Γrms2qmax2 Si.S_{\dot\phi}(\Delta\omega)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\bar R_{\dot\phi}(\tau)\,e^{-j\Delta\omega\tau}\,d\tau=\frac{\Gamma_{rms}^2}{q_{max}^2}\,S_i\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\delta(\tau)e^{-j\Delta\omega\tau}d\tau=\frac{\Gamma_{rms}^2}{q_{max}^2}\,S_i.Sϕ˙​​(Δω)=∫−∞∞​Rˉϕ˙​​(τ)e−jΔωτdτ=qmax2​Γrms2​​Si​∫−∞∞​δ(τ)e−jΔωτdτ=qmax2​Γrms2​​Si​.

The Fourier transform of δ\deltaδ is the constant 111 — so the spectrum of ϕ˙\dot\phiϕ˙​ (the instantaneous frequency perturbation) is white, with strength Γrms2Si/qmax2\Gamma_{rms}^2 S_i/q_{max}^2Γrms2​Si​/qmax2​. Final step: phase is the integral of frequency, and integration in the frequency domain is division by jΔωj\Delta\omegajΔω, so the power spectrum divides by Δω2\Delta\omega^2Δω2:

Sϕ(Δω)=Sϕ˙(Δω)Δω2=Γrms2qmax2⋅SiΔω2[rad2/Hz].S_\phi(\Delta\omega)=\frac{S_{\dot\phi}(\Delta\omega)}{\Delta\omega^2}=\frac{\Gamma_{rms}^2}{q_{max}^2}\cdot\frac{S_i}{\Delta\omega^2}\qquad[\text{rad}^2/\text{Hz}].Sϕ​(Δω)=Δω2Sϕ˙​​(Δω)​=qmax2​Γrms2​​⋅Δω2Si​​[rad2/Hz].

This is verbatim identical to the earlier "clean time-domain version" (the one in the factor-of-2 note), Sϕ=Γrms2Si/(qmax2(2πf)2)S_\phi=\Gamma_{rms}^2S_i/(q_{max}^2(2\pi f)^2)Sϕ​=Γrms2​Si​/(qmax2​(2πf)2) (with Δω=2πf\Delta\omega=2\pi fΔω=2πf).

  • The rigorous origin of 1/f21/f^21/f2: this 1/Δω21/\Delta\omega^21/Δω2 comes entirely from "the one integration ϕ˙→ϕ\dot\phi\to\phiϕ˙​→ϕ" (the 1/(jΔω)1/(j\Delta\omega)1/(jΔω) filter) — word for word the physical intuition at the top of this page, only now it is proven rigorously via Wiener-Khinchin rather than assembled from hand-computed sidebands.
  • The role of the white spectrum: ϕ˙\dot\phiϕ˙​ is white; only ϕ\phiϕ is 1/f21/f^21/f2 — which also explains why the phase is a random walk (the integral of white frequency perturbations === a Wiener process), exactly the starting point of the Lorentzian on the next page.

Rigorous vs heuristic: side-by-side table​

Summary: the rigorous version wields three tools — "cyclostationary autocorrelation → period average → Wiener-Khinchin" — turning both Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​ and 1/f21/f^21/f2 into mechanical inevitabilities. ∑cn2=2Γrms2\sum c_n^2=2\Gamma_{rms}^2∑cn2​=2Γrms2​ is no coincidence, but the Parseval incarnation of the ISF's mean square. This autocorrelation machinery is also precisely the entry point of the next page, lorentzian_linewidth: there, "ϕ˙\dot\phiϕ˙​ white ⇒ ϕ\phiϕ is a random walk" is pushed to its conclusion, yielding the carrier autocorrelation Rx(τ)=12cos⁡(ω0τ)e−D∣τ∣R_x(\tau)=\tfrac12\cos(\omega_0\tau)e^{-D|\tau|}Rx​(τ)=21​cos(ω0​τ)e−D∣τ∣, and Wiener-Khinchin then produces the Lorentzian — resolving the spurious divergence of 1/f21/f^21/f2 as Δω→0\Delta\omega\to0Δω→0. The Sϕ=Γrms2Si/(qmax2Δω2)S_\phi=\Gamma_{rms}^2S_i/(q_{max}^2\Delta\omega^2)Sϕ​=Γrms2​Si​/(qmax2​Δω2) computed in this section is exactly the source of D=Γrms2Si/(4qmax2)D=\Gamma_{rms}^2S_i/(4q_{max}^2)D=Γrms2​Si​/(4qmax2​) there (this site's single-sided bookkeeping is Sϕ=4D/Δω2S_\phi=4D/\Delta\omega^2Sϕ​=4D/Δω2, two-sided 2D/Δω22D/\Delta\omega^22D/Δω2; corrected in v5, reconciliation in diffusion_dictionary).

The relation between Sϕ(f)S_\phi(f)Sϕ​(f) and L(Δf)\mathcal{L}(\Delta f)L(Δf) (dBc/Hz intuition)​

Engineering practice commonly uses two quantities to describe the same thing; you must be able to convert between them:

  • phase PSD Sϕ(f)S_\phi(f)Sϕ​(f): the power spectral density of phase fluctuations, in rad2/Hz\text{rad}^2/\text{Hz}rad2/Hz; integrating over fff gives the phase variance σϕ2\sigma_\phi^2σϕ2​.
  • SSB phase noise L(Δf)\mathcal{L}(\Delta f)L(Δf): single-sideband noise power per Hz relative to the carrier, in dBc/Hz.

Under the small-angle approximation (phase fluctuations far below 1 rad) the two are related by (spec Eq. 16):

L(Δf)≈12Sϕ(Δf).\mathcal{L}(\Delta f)\approx\tfrac12 S_\phi(\Delta f).L(Δf)≈21​Sϕ​(Δf).

Writing the white-noise result in phase-PSD form (clean time-domain derivation, see the section below):

Sϕ(f)=Γrms2qmax2⋅Si(2πf)2[rad2/Hz].S_\phi(f)=\frac{\Gamma_{rms}^2}{q_{max}^2}\cdot\frac{S_i}{(2\pi f)^2}\quad[\text{rad}^2/\text{Hz}].Sϕ​(f)=qmax2​Γrms2​​⋅(2πf)2Si​​[rad2/Hz].
  • dBc/Hz intuition: −100-100−100 dBc/Hz means "at that offset from the carrier, within a 1 Hz bandwidth, the noise power is 101010^{10}1010 times smaller than the carrier". The more negative the number, the cleaner. In the 1/f21/f^21/f2 region, every decade further out improves the dBc/Hz figure by 20 (20 more negative).

The important factor-of-2 teaching note (make sure you understand it)​

If you do the clean time-domain derivation yourself (white noise ×\times× ISF →\to→ integration), you get

Sϕ(f)=Γrms2 Siqmax2(2πf)2,⇒L(Δf)≈12Sϕ=Γrms2qmax2⋅Si2 Δω2.S_\phi(f)=\frac{\Gamma_{rms}^2\,S_i}{q_{max}^2(2\pi f)^2},\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad\mathcal{L}(\Delta f)\approx\tfrac12 S_\phi=\frac{\Gamma_{rms}^2}{q_{max}^2}\cdot\frac{S_i}{2\,\Delta\omega^2}.Sϕ​(f)=qmax2​(2πf)2Γrms2​Si​​,⇒L(Δf)≈21​Sϕ​=qmax2​Γrms2​​⋅2Δω2Si​​.

That is, the denominator is 2 Δω22\,\Delta\omega^22Δω2. But [P1] Eq.(21) has 4 Δω24\,\Delta\omega^24Δω2. They differ by a factor of 2.

  • The gap comes from the SSB (single-sideband) bookkeeping convention: whether all of the phase-fluctuation power is charged to "a single sideband" or "split evenly across both sidebands", and whether in2‾/Δf\overline{i_n^2}/\Delta fin2​​/Δf is a single-sided or two-sided PSD — any inconsistency in definitions produces a factor of 2.
  • This is a famous minor controversy in the literature; the constant lands somewhere between /2/2/2 and /4/4/4 across textbooks/papers.
  • The key point: it does not affect the Γrms2/qmax2\Gamma_{rms}^2/q_{max}^2Γrms2​/qmax2​ scaling at all, nor the −20-20−20 dB/decade slope. Design work looks at scaling and slope; that ±3\pm3±3 dB constant is naturally absorbed during measurement calibration.
  • This site's lab_06 numerical simulation uses the clean time-domain version Sϕ=Γrms2Si/(qmax2(2πf)2)S_\phi=\Gamma_{rms}^2 S_i/(q_{max}^2(2\pi f)^2)Sϕ​=Γrms2​Si​/(qmax2​(2πf)2), so it differs from Eq.(21) by this factor of 2 — expected and taught, not a bug.

One sentence to remember: slope and scaling are physics; the constant 2 is bookkeeping. Do not lose sleep over that 2.

Numerical example (canonical Example B, step by step with units)​

Example B: f0=5f_0=5f0​=5 GHz, Δf=1\Delta f=1Δf=1 MHz, qmax=1q_{max}=1qmax​=1 pC, Γrms=0.5\Gamma_{rms}=0.5Γrms​=0.5, Si=10−24 A2/HzS_i=10^{-24}\,\text{A}^2/\text{Hz}Si​=10−24A2/Hz. Use [P1] Eq.(21).

Step 1: compute the offset angular frequency.

Δω=2πΔf=2π×106=6.283×106 rad/s,Δω2=3.948×1013 rad2/s2.\Delta\omega=2\pi\Delta f=2\pi\times10^{6}=6.283\times10^{6}\ \text{rad/s},\qquad\Delta\omega^2=3.948\times10^{13}\ \text{rad}^2/\text{s}^2.Δω=2πΔf=2π×106=6.283×106 rad/s,Δω2=3.948×1013 rad2/s2.

Step 2: compute Γrms2/qmax2\Gamma_{rms}^2/q_{max}^2Γrms2​/qmax2​.

Γrms2qmax2=0.25(10−12)2=0.2510−24=2.5×1023 C−2.\frac{\Gamma_{rms}^2}{q_{max}^2}=\frac{0.25}{(10^{-12})^2}=\frac{0.25}{10^{-24}}=2.5\times10^{23}\ \text{C}^{-2}.qmax2​Γrms2​​=(10−12)20.25​=10−240.25​=2.5×1023 C−2.

Step 3: compute Si/(4Δω2)S_i/(4\Delta\omega^2)Si​/(4Δω2).

Si4 Δω2=10−244×3.948×1013=10−241.579×1014=6.332×10−39.\frac{S_i}{4\,\Delta\omega^2}=\frac{10^{-24}}{4\times3.948\times10^{13}}=\frac{10^{-24}}{1.579\times10^{14}}=6.332\times10^{-39}.4Δω2Si​​=4×3.948×101310−24​=1.579×101410−24​=6.332×10−39.

L(1 MHz)=10log⁡10(1.583×10−15)=−148.0 dBc/Hz.\mathcal{L}(1\,\text{MHz})=10\log_{10}(1.583\times10^{-15})=-148.0\ \text{dBc/Hz}.L(1MHz)=10log10​(1.583×10−15)=−148.0 dBc/Hz.
  • Feel for the number: this is the theoretical floor for a "single ideal white-noise source", about −148-148−148 dBc/Hz @ 1 MHz. Real circuits have multiple noise sources (several transistors, tail, load), cyclostationary gating (see effective_isf), and close-in flicker upconversion (see flicker_noise_upconversion); actual values are higher (closer to 0).
  • Cross-page consistency: with the clean time-domain version (/2/2/2 instead of /4/4/4), the same parameters give ≈−145.0\approx-145.0≈−145.0 dBc/Hz — exactly 3 dB apart (10log⁡10210\log_{10}210log10​2) — the numerical face of the factor-of-2 above.

Core Python (full script: simulations/lab_06_white_noise_phase_noise.py):

import numpy as np
from simulations.common.noise_utils import white_noise, estimate_psd
from simulations.common.isf_utils import gamma_lc_ideal, gamma_rms, apply_isf_weighting

# white-noise current -> ISF weighting -> cumulative integration -> phase -> PSD
i_n = white_noise(n=2**20, psd=1e-4, fs=256.0, rng=np.random.default_rng(0))
phi = apply_isf_weighting(t, i_n, gamma_lc_ideal, qmax=1.0, omega0=2*np.pi*1.0)
f, S_phi = estimate_psd(phi, fs=256.0, nperseg=4096)   # measures -20 dB/dec

Worked examples​

The two problems below follow the strict format: problem → step-by-step substitution (with units) → result → dimension check → one-line Python verification. The first reuses the canonical Example B (spec §8); the second uses a different set of numbers for practice. Both apply [P1] Eq.(21).

Example 3 (adding two noise sources): A real oscillator is never driven by just one noise source. This example demonstrates multi-source superposition — two independent white-noise sources hitting the same ideal-LC node at once. How do we combine them into a total phase noise?

Problem setup. Reuse the oscillator parameters from Example 1 (f0=5f_0=5f0​=5 GHz, Δf=1\Delta f=1Δf=1 MHz, qmax=1q_{max}=1qmax​=1 pC). Superpose two statistically independent white-noise current sources on the node:

  • Device A (e.g. the main transconductor, which sees the full ISF): ΓA,rms=0.5\Gamma_{A,rms}=0.5ΓA,rms​=0.5, Si,A=in,A2‾/Δf=1×10−24 A2/HzS_{i,A}=\overline{i_{n,A}^2}/\Delta f=1\times10^{-24}\ \text{A}^2/\text{Hz}Si,A​=in,A2​​/Δf=1×10−24 A2/Hz.
  • Device B (a tail-current-source-type device, which only contributes noise during part of the cycle because of cyclostationary gating — see effective_isf and Γeff=Γα\Gamma_{eff}=\Gamma\alphaΓeff​=Γα): effective Γeff,B,rms=0.25\Gamma_{eff,B,rms}=0.25Γeff,B,rms​=0.25 (half of A's — an illustrative value), but with larger current-noise power Si,B=4×10−24 A2/HzS_{i,B}=4\times10^{-24}\ \text{A}^2/\text{Hz}Si,B​=4×10−24 A2/Hz (e.g. a device biased with a larger current).

The two are distinct physical noise sources and are independent (uncorrelated), so the question is: what is the combined Ltotal(1MHz)\mathcal{L}_{total}(1\text{MHz})Ltotal​(1MHz)?

Step 0: why independent sources add in SϕS_\phiSϕ​ (power), not in dB. Each noise source is separately weighted by its (possibly different) ISF and independently integrated into a phase perturbation ϕA(t)\phi_A(t)ϕA​(t), ϕB(t)\phi_B(t)ϕB​(t) (see [P1] Eq.(11)); the total excess phase at the node is the linear superposition ϕ(t)=ϕA(t)+ϕB(t)\phi(t)=\phi_A(t)+\phi_B(t)ϕ(t)=ϕA​(t)+ϕB​(t). For independent (uncorrelated) random processes, the variance/power spectral density adds and the cross term has zero expectation:

Sϕ,total(Δω)=⟨(ϕA+ϕB)(ϕA+ϕB)⟩spectrum=Sϕ,A(Δω)+Sϕ,B(Δω)+2 Re⟨ϕAϕB∗⟩⏟=0 (independent).S_{\phi,total}(\Delta\omega)=\big\langle(\phi_A+\phi_B)(\phi_A+\phi_B)\big\rangle_{\text{spectrum}}=S_{\phi,A}(\Delta\omega)+S_{\phi,B}(\Delta\omega)+\underbrace{2\,\text{Re}\langle\phi_A\phi_B^*\rangle}_{=0\ (\text{independent})}.Sϕ,total​(Δω)=⟨(ϕA​+ϕB​)(ϕA​+ϕB​)⟩spectrum​=Sϕ,A​(Δω)+Sϕ,B​(Δω)+=0 (independent)2Re⟨ϕA​ϕB∗​⟩​​.

This is the "one-line rule" for this problem: independent sources add in SϕS_\phiSϕ​ (linear power) — you must never add or average two dBc/Hz numbers directly. You have to convert each back to linear, add, and only then take a single 10log⁡1010\log_{10}10log10​.

Step 1: compute Device A alone (same recipe as Example 1, using [P1] Eq.(21)).

LA=10log⁡10 ⁣(ΓA,rms2qmax2⋅Si,A4 Δω2),Δω=2π×106=6.283×106 rad/s, Δω2=3.948×1013.\mathcal{L}_A=10\log_{10}\!\left(\frac{\Gamma_{A,rms}^2}{q_{max}^2}\cdot\frac{S_{i,A}}{4\,\Delta\omega^2}\right),\qquad \Delta\omega=2\pi\times10^6=6.283\times10^6\ \text{rad/s},\ \Delta\omega^2=3.948\times10^{13}.LA​=10log10​(qmax2​ΓA,rms2​​⋅4Δω2Si,A​​),Δω=2π×106=6.283×106 rad/s, Δω2=3.948×1013. ΓA,rms2qmax2=0.2510−24=2.5×1023 C−2,Si,A4Δω2=10−241.579×1014=6.332×10−39.\frac{\Gamma_{A,rms}^2}{q_{max}^2}=\frac{0.25}{10^{-24}}=2.5\times10^{23}\ \text{C}^{-2},\qquad \frac{S_{i,A}}{4\Delta\omega^2}=\frac{10^{-24}}{1.579\times10^{14}}=6.332\times10^{-39}.qmax2​ΓA,rms2​​=10−240.25​=2.5×1023 C−2,4Δω2Si,A​​=1.579×101410−24​=6.332×10−39.

Linear value inside the parentheses: ℓA=2.5×1023×6.332×10−39=1.583×10−15\ell_A=2.5\times10^{23}\times6.332\times10^{-39}=1.583\times10^{-15}ℓA​=2.5×1023×6.332×10−39=1.583×10−15, so LA=10log⁡10(1.583×10−15)≈−148.0 dBc/Hz\mathcal{L}_A=10\log_{10}(1.583\times10^{-15})\approx-148.0\ \text{dBc/Hz}LA​=10log10​(1.583×10−15)≈−148.0 dBc/Hz (matches Example 1 — same parameters).

Step 2: compute Device B alone (same formula, with Γ→Γeff,B,rms\Gamma\to\Gamma_{eff,B,rms}Γ→Γeff,B,rms​, Si→Si,BS_i\to S_{i,B}Si​→Si,B​).

Γeff,B,rms2qmax2=0.25210−24=0.062510−24=6.25×1022 C−2,Si,B4Δω2=4×10−241.579×1014=2.533×10−38.\frac{\Gamma_{eff,B,rms}^2}{q_{max}^2}=\frac{0.25^2}{10^{-24}}=\frac{0.0625}{10^{-24}}=6.25\times10^{22}\ \text{C}^{-2},\qquad \frac{S_{i,B}}{4\Delta\omega^2}=\frac{4\times10^{-24}}{1.579\times10^{14}}=2.533\times10^{-38}.qmax2​Γeff,B,rms2​​=10−240.252​=10−240.0625​=6.25×1022 C−2,4Δω2Si,B​​=1.579×10144×10−24​=2.533×10−38.

Linear value: ℓB=6.25×1022×2.533×10−38=1.583×10−15\ell_B=6.25\times10^{22}\times2.533\times10^{-38}=1.583\times10^{-15}ℓB​=6.25×1022×2.533×10−38=1.583×10−15, so LB=10log⁡10(1.583×10−15)≈−148.0 dBc/Hz\mathcal{L}_B=10\log_{10}(1.583\times10^{-15})\approx-148.0\ \text{dBc/Hz}LB​=10log10​(1.583×10−15)≈−148.0 dBc/Hz.

"You'd think A dominates — it doesn't": at first glance Γeff,B,rms=0.25\Gamma_{eff,B,rms}=0.25Γeff,B,rms​=0.25 is only half of ΓA,rms=0.5\Gamma_{A,rms}=0.5ΓA,rms​=0.5, so intuition suggests Device B's ISF-weight term Γeff,B,rms2/qmax2\Gamma_{eff,B,rms}^2/q_{max}^2Γeff,B,rms2​/qmax2​ is 4×4\times4× smaller (−6-6−6 dB) and B should be completely swamped by A and safely ignored. But Device B's current noise Si,BS_{i,B}Si,B​ happens to be exactly 4×4\times4× larger (+6+6+6 dB) — the two ±6\pm6±6 dB effects exactly cancel, giving LA=LB≈−148.0\mathcal{L}_A=\mathcal{L}_B\approx-148.0LA​=LB​≈−148.0 dBc/Hz: B is just as strong as A and contributes equally — it cannot be neglected. This is exactly the trap you fall into by judging a noise source's contribution from Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​ alone: what actually sets the contribution is the product Γrms2⋅Si\Gamma_{rms}^2\cdot S_iΓrms2​⋅Si​, and both factors must be considered together.

Step 3: power-sum (add in the linear domain, not in dB).

Ltotal=10log⁡10(ℓA+ℓB)=10log⁡10(1.583×10−15+1.583×10−15)=10log⁡10(3.166×10−15).\mathcal{L}_{total}=10\log_{10}\big(\ell_A+\ell_B\big)=10\log_{10}\big(1.583\times10^{-15}+1.583\times10^{-15}\big)=10\log_{10}(3.166\times10^{-15}).Ltotal​=10log10​(ℓA​+ℓB​)=10log10​(1.583×10−15+1.583×10−15)=10log10​(3.166×10−15).

Cross-check with the equivalent "dB-domain power-combining formula" (convert each back to linear via 10L/1010^{L/10}10L/10, add, then take a single 10log⁡1010\log_{10}10log10​):

Ltotal=10log⁡10 ⁣(10LA/10+10LB/10)=10log⁡10 ⁣(10−148.0/10+10−148.0/10).\mathcal{L}_{total}=10\log_{10}\!\Big(10^{\mathcal{L}_A/10}+10^{\mathcal{L}_B/10}\Big)=10\log_{10}\!\Big(10^{-148.0/10}+10^{-148.0/10}\Big).Ltotal​=10log10​(10LA​/10+10LB​/10)=10log10​(10−148.0/10+10−148.0/10).

Result: Ltotal(1 MHz)≈−145.0 dBc/Hz\mathcal{L}_{total}(1\,\text{MHz})\approx-145.0\ \text{dBc/Hz}Ltotal​(1MHz)≈−145.0 dBc/Hz.

  • What just happened arithmetically: AAA and BBB have equal power, so together they give exactly twice the power ⇒10log⁡102≈3.01\Rightarrow 10\log_{10}2\approx3.01⇒10log10​2≈3.01 dB, so Ltotal≈LA+3.0 dB=−148.0+3.0=−145.0\mathcal{L}_{total}\approx\mathcal{L}_A+3.0\ \text{dB}=-148.0+3.0=-145.0Ltotal​≈LA​+3.0 dB=−148.0+3.0=−145.0 dBc/Hz. Device B's contribution to the total noise, expressed as "how much worse than A alone," is X = 3.0 dB — not the 0 dB you'd wrongly conclude by reasoning that "Γeff,B,rms\Gamma_{eff,B,rms}Γeff,B,rms​ is only half" and therefore negligible.
  • One-line rule (memorize this): uncorrelated (independent) noise sources add in SϕS_\phiSϕ​/power — never add dBc/Hz numbers directly, and never average them. Two equal-power sources combine to ×2=+3.0\times2=+3.0×2=+3.0 dB, not +6+6+6 dB (that would only happen for coherent/voltage-amplitude addition; white-noise sources here are uncorrelated).

Dimension check: ℓA\ell_AℓA​ and ℓB\ell_BℓB​ each have the form Γrms2/qmax2⋅Si/(4Δω2)\Gamma_{rms}^2/q_{max}^2\cdot S_i/(4\Delta\omega^2)Γrms2​/qmax2​⋅Si​/(4Δω2), just as in Examples 1 and 2, and both reduce to s\text{s}s (per-Hz, see the dimension check in Example 1) — only quantities with the same dimension may be added; the sum is still s\text{s}s, and after 10log⁡1010\log_{10}10log10​ it reads as dBc/Hz ✓.

import numpy as np

qmax = 1e-12                       # C
dw = 2*np.pi*1e6                   # rad/s (offset Δf = 1 MHz)

# Device A: main transconductor, sees the full ISF
gamma_A, Si_A = 0.5, 1e-24         # (–, A^2/Hz)
# Device B: tail device; smaller effective Gamma_eff,rms after cyclostationary gating, but larger current noise
gamma_effB, Si_B = 0.25, 4e-24     # (–, A^2/Hz)

def bracket(gamma_rms, Si, qmax, dw):
    return (gamma_rms**2 / qmax**2) * (Si / (4 * dw**2))   # linear value inside [P1] Eq.(21)

ell_A = bracket(gamma_A, Si_A, qmax, dw)
ell_B = bracket(gamma_effB, Si_B, qmax, dw)
L_A = 10*np.log10(ell_A)
L_B = 10*np.log10(ell_B)
print(round(L_A, 1), "dBc/Hz  (A alone)")   # -> -148.0 dBc/Hz
print(round(L_B, 1), "dBc/Hz  (B alone)")   # -> -148.0 dBc/Hz

# Correct approach: sum the power (linear S_phi), then take one log; never add two dB numbers
L_total_via_linear = 10*np.log10(ell_A + ell_B)
L_total_via_powersum = 10*np.log10(10**(L_A/10) + 10**(L_B/10))   # equivalent form, for cross-check
print(round(L_total_via_linear, 1), "dBc/Hz  (A+B power-summed)")     # -> -145.0 dBc/Hz
print(round(L_total_via_powersum, 1), "dBc/Hz  (cross-check)")        # -> -145.0 dBc/Hz

X_dB = L_total_via_linear - L_A   # degradation contributed by B: here A and B contribute equally
print(round(X_dB, 1), "dB  (B's contribution, even though Gamma_eff,B,rms is only half of Gamma_A,rms)")  # -> 3.0 dB

(This example continues the [P1] Eq.(21) SSB /4/4/4 convention; both sources use the same formula, each with its own Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​ (or Γeff,rms\Gamma_{eff,rms}Γeff,rms​) and SiS_iSi​, and are summed in power. Using the lab_06 clean time-domain /2/2/2 version instead would shift LA\mathcal{L}_ALA​, LB\mathcal{L}_BLB​, and Ltotal\mathcal{L}_{total}Ltotal​ all up by 333 dB together — leaving the 3.0 dB gap between them unchanged. This echoes the factor-of-2 note above: the constant convention does not affect scaling/relative relationships. The full rule for multi-source superposition and the derivation of the cyclostationary Γeff\Gamma_{eff}Γeff​ are in effective_isf; full libraries: simulations/common/noise_utils.py, simulations/common/isf_utils.py.)

Key takeaways​

  • White noise is flat; the 1/f21/f^21/f2 slope comes entirely from the phase integrator's 1/ω21/\omega^21/ω2 — the ISF only sets the size of the weight.
  • Derivation chain: Eq.(19) summation → Eq.(20) Parseval (∑cn2=2Γrms2\sum c_n^2=2\Gamma_{rms}^2∑cn2​=2Γrms2​) → Eq.(21) signature result.
  • L∝Γrms2/qmax2⋅Si/Δω2\mathcal{L}\propto\Gamma_{rms}^2/q_{max}^2\cdot S_i/\Delta\omega^2L∝Γrms2​/qmax2​⋅Si​/Δω2; in design, increase qmaxq_{max}qmax​ and reduce Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​.
  • L≈12Sϕ\mathcal{L}\approx\frac12 S_\phiL≈21​Sϕ​; the 1/f21/f^21/f2 region improves by 20 dB per decade.
  • Factor-of-2: the clean time-domain version has /(2Δω2)/(2\Delta\omega^2)/(2Δω2); [P1] Eq.(21) has /(4Δω2)/(4\Delta\omega^2)/(4Δω2); the factor 2 comes from SSB bookkeeping and does not affect scaling/slope.
  • Canonical Example B: a single white-noise source gives ≈−148\approx-148≈−148 dBc/Hz @ 1 MHz (time-domain version −145-145−145, 3 dB apart).
